1. Core Clinical Tension: A 44-year-old immunocompetent woman presents with 2 months of subacute intermittent abdominal pain, night sweats, and peritoneal signs, found to have ascites, marked nodular peritoneal/omental thickening, and an irregular hepatic mass invading liver parenchyma. This complex constellation closely simulates advanced peritoneal carcinomatosis or a pyogenic liver abscess with secondary peritonitis, requiring differentiation from extrapulmonary tuberculous infection.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs following initial triage, baseline laboratory and tumor marker tests, chest CT, and abdominal contrast CT/ultrasound defining the hepatic mass and nodular peritoneal thickening, strictly before ultrasound-guided liver biopsy, tuberculin skin testing, and PCR analysis.
3. Differential Distinctions: Pyogenic liver abscess typically presents acutely with high spiking fever and leukocytosis, whereas this patient had a 2-month history, normal leukocyte count, and sterile blood cultures. Peritoneal carcinomatosis and hepatic neoplasm were strong considerations given extensive nodular peritoneal thickening and ascites, but serum tumor markers (CEA, CA-19.9, CA-125, AFP) were completely normal, and histology showed granulomatous rather than malignant architecture.
case_prompt:
A 44-year-old woman, employed as a company clerk and residing in Luzhou City, Sichuan Province, China, presented to the hospital with a 2-month history of intermittent abdominal pain lasting from several minutes to several hours per episode. The pain was accompanied by decreased appetite, low-grade fever, and night sweats. She reported no nausea, vomiting, alterations in bowel habits, chills, or cough with sputum production. She had no past medical history of liver disease or immunocompromising illness, no history of weight loss over the past year, no recent travel outside Luzhou, and no contact with animals or known ill contacts.

Physical examination on admission:
- Vital signs: respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, body temperature 36.5°C, heart rate 70 beats/min, blood pressure 118/78 mmHg, oxygen saturation 33% on room air (as documented).
- Abdomen: tender to palpation in the periumbilical and right lower abdominal regions, with positive rebound tenderness. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory evaluation:
- Complete blood count: total leukocyte count 7.01 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 5.56 × 10^9/L), platelet count 229 × 10^9/L
- Inflammatory markers: C-reactive protein (CRP) 10.65 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 33 mm/h
- Renal panel and electrolytes: urea 5.0 mmol/L, creatinine 72 µmol/L, uric acid 231 µmol/L, GFR 100 mL/min, potassium 4.15 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, chloride 105.2 mmol/L
- Liver function tests: ALT 80 U/L, AST 78 U/L, total bilirubin 17 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 8.6 µmol/L, indirect bilirubin 8.4 µmol/L, albumin 35 g/L
- Blood cultures: negative for bacterial growth
- Tumor markers: CEA, CA-19.9, CA-125, and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) were all within normal limits
- HIV serology was negative

Imaging studies:
- Chest CT was normal.
- Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a small volume of ascites in the lesser omental sac and abdominal/pelvic cavities (predominantly pelvic); extensive smooth and nodular thickening of the greater omentum, mesentery, and peritoneum; a round, low-density, non-enhancing 0.8 cm lesion in the right anterior hepatic lobe; patchy arterial phase enhancement in the left medial hepatic lobe becoming isodense in the venous phase; and an irregular mass measuring approximately 4.1 × 3.1 cm in the right anterior space of the liver, invading the right anterior hepatic lobe.
- Abdominal ultrasound of the right hepatic lobe revealed a cystic dark region measuring 3.7 × 2.1 cm.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Suggested by CT and ultrasound findings of an irregular right hepatic mass invading parenchyma with abscess-like characteristics, but argued against by the prolonged subacute 2-month course, normal leukocyte count, negative blood cultures, and absence of acute suppurative changes on aspiration.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The hepatic CT showed an irregular mass of approximately 4.1 cm x 3.1 cm in the right anterior space of the liver, part of which invaded the right anterior lobe of the liver (Figure 1a). The findings are consistent with an infection complicated by abscess formation involving the anterior segment of the right hepatic lobe.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Extensive nodular omental, mesenteric, and peritoneal thickening accompanied by ascites and a hepatic mass raised strong suspicion for metastatic malignant disease, but serum tumor markers (CEA, CA-19.9, CA-125, AFP) were strictly normal, and biopsy confirmed a benign chronic granulomatous etiology.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The carcinoembryonic antigen, CA-19.9, CA-125, and a-fetoprotein serum tumor markers were all within normal limits.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Ultrasound-guided percutaneous biopsy of the hepatic mass demonstrated chronic granulomatous inflammation, accompanied by a positive tuberculin skin test and positive real-time PCR detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex DNA in aspirated pus, confirming hepatic tuberculosis with tuberculous peritonitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Ultrasound-guided biopsy of the lesion was done, which showed chronic granulomatous inflammation suggestive of tuberculosis (Figure 1c). The tuberculin test was positive. TB-DNA real-time PCR performed on the aspirated pus was positive, confirming the presence of M. tuberculosis complex DNA.

editor_comments: Case distilled strictly adhering to Stanford MedCaseReasoning principles. The phrase attributing peritoneal findings to tuberculosis was excised from case prompt to eliminate spoilers. Verified exact quotes.
